title: DNS: names into numbers
story:
Machines are reachable by number and people cannot hold numbers in their heads, so something has to map one to the other. The first solution was a single file listing every host, copied around. That works while one person can maintain it, and stops working the moment the network outgrows a single administrator — not for technical reasons but organisational ones, which is the shape of this whole lesson.

Mockapetris published the design as RFC 1034 in November 1987, obsoleting the earlier RFCs from 1983 on the basis of experience with several implementations. The stated goal is worth reading closely because it is not primarily about lookup: to provide a mechanism for naming resources such that the names are usable across different hosts, networks, protocol families, internets and administrative organisations. That last item is the difficult one. The problem being solved is that no single party can be allowed to approve every name.

The answer is delegation, and the hierarchy exists to make delegation possible. The shared idea across the competing proposals that preceded it was a hierarchical name space roughly corresponding to organisational structure, with the full stop marking boundaries between levels. Each level is administered by whoever owns it and can delegate the level below without consulting anyone above. The database is distributed because the authority is distributed; the technical design is downstream of the political one.

What that costs is that a lookup is now a distributed query taking several steps, which would be intolerable if performed every time. So answers are cached, with a lifetime attached by whoever published them. Caching is not an optimisation bolted on afterwards — it is what makes the design viable, and it is the source of essentially every operational surprise here. A cached answer is correct until the underlying record changes and stale thereafter, and the system has no way to reach out and correct it. You wait for it to expire.

Which produces the behaviour everyone eventually meets: a change is live for you, and not yet live for a colleague, and both of you are right. The lifetime you set on a record is a decision about how long you are willing to be wrong after a change, traded against how much lookup traffic you want to carry — and it has to be lowered in advance of a change, because lowering it afterwards only affects caches that have already expired.

The design was also made deliberately extensible, on the explicit argument that future developments could not be predicted. That judgement has held up: the system now carries record types for purposes nobody in 1987 was contemplating.

problem.name: Hierarchical delegated naming
problem.shape: Human-usable names must map to machine addresses, and no single party can be allowed to administer every name.
tell: a change has propagated to some users and not others
a name must survive the machine behind it being replaced
the mapping is maintained by many independent organisations
a cutover is planned and nobody has discussed record lifetimes
problem.move: Treat the lifetime on a record as the length of time you are willing to be wrong after a change, and lower it in advance of any cutover rather than during one. Expect resolution to be cached at layers you do not control, and design changeovers so that both the old and new answers work during the overlap.
problem.invariant: Authority is delegated down the hierarchy, and answers are cached with a publisher-set lifetime. A cached answer cannot be recalled — it can only be allowed to expire.
problem.breaks: The lifetime governs caches that honour it, and the path from a user to you contains resolvers, operating systems, runtimes and applications that may cache independently and for longer. So the record's lifetime is a lower bound on how long a stale answer can persist rather than a guarantee.

cost.time: a multi-step distributed query on a cache miss, which is why the first request to a new name is measurably slower
cost.space: caches at every layer, which is the mechanism and the problem
cost.beats: a single central registry, which cannot scale organisationally, and hard-coded addresses, which break whenever the machine behind a name changes

worked.problem: Why can a change be live for you and not yet live for somebody else?
worked.reasoning:
Because the answer they are using was cached before you made the change, and nothing in the design can reach out and correct it.

Start from why caching is not optional. A resolution is a distributed query that walks down a delegated hierarchy, taking several exchanges. Performing that on every use would be intolerable, so answers are cached with a lifetime set by whoever published them. Caching is what makes the design viable rather than an optimisation applied to it.

The consequence is that a published answer is a promise for a fixed duration. Once handed out, it exists in caches you cannot enumerate and cannot revoke. You change the record; every cache still holding the old one continues to serve it until its own copy expires. So during that window some users have the new answer and some have the old, and both are behaving correctly.

Why this is structural rather than a shortcoming: the design exists because no single party can administer every name — the goal was names usable across different hosts, networks, protocol families, internets and administrative organisations. Delegation is the answer to that, and delegation means the parties holding your cached answer are not yours to command. A recall mechanism would require exactly the central coordination the design was built to avoid.

The practical handling follows directly. Lower the lifetime well before a change, so that by the time you cut over, cached copies are short-lived — and note it must be in advance, because lowering it afterwards only reaches caches that have already expired and re-fetched. Then keep both destinations working through the overlap, because you cannot know when the last stale copy drains. Raise the lifetime again afterwards to recover the traffic saving.

The part I would flag as the real trap is that the lifetime is a lower bound rather than a guarantee. The path between a user and you contains recursive resolvers, operating system caches, language runtimes and long-lived application connections, and some of them cache for their own reasons and their own durations. Some ignore the lifetime entirely. So the honest plan assumes stale answers persist longer than the record says, and designs the cutover so that being wrong for a while is survivable rather than trying to make the window zero.

problem.practice: Look up the lifetime on a record your system depends on and work out how long a stale answer could be served after you change it. Then plan a cutover on paper: when you would lower it, when you would change the record, and how long both destinations must keep working.

beats.broke: Machines are reachable by number and people cannot remember numbers, and the first solution — one shared file listing every host — cannot be maintained once the network outgrows a single administrator.
beats.fix: Give the name space a hierarchy mirroring organisational structure, delegate each level to whoever owns it, and distribute the database so no one party has to know or approve the whole thing.
beats.cost: A lookup becomes a multi-step distributed query, so answers are cached — and a cached answer is stale from the moment the record changes until it expires.

interview.q: Why can a change be live for you and not yet live for somebody else?
interview.trap: Treating it as propagation delay that will resolve shortly. Nothing is propagating — old answers are being served from caches that cannot be recalled, and the record's lifetime is a lower bound on how long that lasts rather than a guarantee.
interview.answer:
Because the answer they are using was cached before the change, and nothing in the design can reach out and correct it.
